lines: Make some money through trade contracts or freelancer jobs, but on freelance runs you have to buy the goods yourself.
Always keep enough fuel cells racked up before you undock for a long leg.
Delivery contracts load their own crate straight into your hold; just make sure you have the cubic metres free.
If you jettison a delivery crate in deep space, that contract is gone for good.
At a freelance destination you can take market price or try squeezing ten or twenty percent more if you feel lucky.
Check the Starmap card while you are docked; reading the whole system page costs zero clicks.
Every station you dock at unlocks station-to-station survey trades with the ports you visited before.
Trade boards roll over every hundred actions, so old routes give way to fresh ones as the voyage goes on.
Right-click the fuel or energy gauge whenever you want to crack a fuel cell in a hurry.
Your drive loses a little condition every four clicks, so peek into the Engine Room before it quits mid-crossing.
Seat all three canisters in the O2 Filter Room before starting the bank, or cabin air will turn sour fast.
Starting a full filter bank pushes your ongoing tasks forward without even advancing the world clock.
Keep a couple of repair kits aboard; an open incident only gets nastier the longer you ignore it.
When hull drops to sixty percent or below, mechanical trouble starts bleeding your fuel right alongside it.
Low energy pauses powered work, and below sixty percent an electrical fault chews on your shields too.
Crew eat cooked meals off the galley counter, not raw dry rations out of the locker.
An assigned engineer, cook, and filter hand will run their rooms on their own while you mind the chart.
Putting a trained navigator on duty trims your fuel burn every time you depart.
HOLD stops the ship right where it stands between worlds if you suddenly rethink your destination.
You can plot a new course mid-flight without finishing the old leg first, provided the fuel holds out.
Deep-scan local worlds and package the surveys in the Science Room to bump their price before selling.
Crates in the cargo hold jostle loose every five to ten clicks, so sort them back down when you have a breather.
Workshop turns salvage into repair kits, Recyclers make O2 canisters, and Fuel Reserve refines spare cells.
Hydroponics can press produce into dry rations when station pantries are charging too much.
Two free crew members sharing a meal in Recreation lifts morale without costing a single shiplet.
Medical Bay treatment spends a medkit and power, while a rest order in Crew Quarters only takes time.
Check the tavern every fifty actions or so; a fresh crowd of hands rotates through looking for a berth.
Chatting at the bar turns up the best sell price and cheapest buy on this station's counter.
Opening tabs, flipping chart layers, and reading the Ship's Handbook are all completely free.
Remember crew wages tick on the action clock, so keep a little cushion in your purse between runs.
Don't forget the Rewards logbook; claiming earned commendations hands over free shiplets and supplies.
Cargo bay refits at the Shipyard carry right over if you upgrade to a bigger hull later.
Buying a second ship lets you park your old hull and switch back whenever you feel nostalgic.
Stand Watch in Navigation advances the clock by one click even when your hold is packed to the rafters.
Compare prices between ports: buy where a good is cheap and haul it somewhere that actually misses it.
Hit the disk icon and save your slot before jumping somewhere with suspiciously cheap fuel.
Risky cargo pays handsomely right up until you remember why everybody else left it on the dock.
The Power Bus and Shield Array can trade energy and shields back and forth, minus a little conversion loss.
Bridge WARP covers ground fast, and its green bar refills gradually as you spend ordinary clicks.
Salvage bays work while a crossing is running, provided you have spare energy and three cubic metres open.
Docking collars report green, though collar four still makes a noise like a kettle full of bolts.
Somebody left a half-eaten ration bar on the transponder console again, and I am not admitting it was me.
The vending machine by bay two claims it serves espresso, though chemically it is closer to warm paint.
My cassette deck ate side B of my favourite synth tape five minutes before your hull cleared the buoys.
I watered the fern in harbour control all week before the quartermaster told me it was moulded vinyl.
Never trust a freighter captain whose boots are cleaner than his navigation glass.
There is an orange cat asleep on the warm telemetry rack, so if your signal wobbles, she rolled over.
Station rule seven: no welding in the corridor, no gambling on airlock timers, and no whistling on night shift.
I just stamped forty-two cargo manifests in purple ink and somehow got forty-three smudges on my sleeve.
Today's dockside horoscope was read off a faulty oscilloscope, and it predicts mild static and good soup.
Have you ever noticed every crate in the galaxy is stencilled THIS SIDE UP on at least two wrong sides?
If you hear rhythmic tapping in the bulkhead, that is just maintenance arguing with a stubborn vent flap.
I bet the signal clerk two shiplets you would dock on the first approach, so thanks for the free lunch.
Low-gravity laundry is a scam; three left socks went into the drum and only a wrench came back out.
Our harbour beacon turns ninety cycles old next month and still blinks half a beat faster when it is proud.
Do spaceships dream when parked, or do they just sit there ticking softly as the hull cools off?
The noodle stall on deck C puts real scallions on top whenever an inner-lane hauler drops off greens.
My clipboard has six coloured pens clipped to it and somehow only the chewed blue one actually writes.
Sometimes I salute the wrong viewport and end up greeting an automated tug that does not even have eyes.
A prospector tried to pay his berthing fee with a very shiny rock; honestly, I almost took it.
Fluorescent tube twelve only stops buzzing if you look directly at it, so I can never blink at my desk.
Every spacer swears their next run is a quiet milk route, right before buying three medkits and a wrench.
Whoever tuned the lobby radio between two frequencies invented a brand-new genre of soothing hiss.
I tried counting all the rivets around airlock B on a slow watch and lost track somewhere past four hundred.
Please wipe the stardust off your boots; the corridor buffer droid takes muddy footprints personally.
My shift supervisor says enthusiasm does not replace proper dock paperwork, so now I stamp forms enthusiastically.
Out past the marker buoys everything looks so still you almost forget how fast we are all falling sideways.
Rumour says one station out here actually makes decent toast, though nobody ever writes down the coordinates.
I keep a lucky brass washer in my jacket pocket; no idea which machine is missing it, and I refuse to ask.
Three different crews came through today swearing they saw a comet shaped exactly like a soup ladle.
If your air filters smell faintly of pine needles, congratulations, you got the fancy batch.
Nothing beats the sound of fresh magnetic clamps locking home after a long quiet crossing.
I reorganised the spare gasket drawer by size, then by colour, and now nobody including me can find anything.
An old navigator told me stars never actually twinkle in vacuum; they just wait until you squint.
Dock coffee has three official strengths: lantern oil, bulkhead stripper, and Tuesday morning.
Hold on, my scrunchie was crooked - okay, official station greeting posture fully restored.
Why do buttons on ship consoles always feel ten times better to press when they make a chunky click?
The customs printer ran out of ribbon, so if your receipt looks faint just hold it up to an amber lamp.
I once tried learning accordion for the station talent night; they promoted me to a very distant airlock.
Keep an eye on belts and old wrecks when trading; even lonely outposts out there still need water and parts.
Ice worlds and gas-giant rigs pay nicely for fresh greens if you can haul a crate out to the cold bands.
Outer-band destinations take a little longer to reach, though their payout carries a small distance bonus.
I swear the dock clock runs slower during the last twenty minutes before warm buns hit the mess counter.
Somebody drew a tiny smiley face in the frost on the cryo-pipe, and now it is a protected station landmark.
Be kind to your hull plates; they are the only thing keeping all the interesting air on the inside.
My favourite ships are the scuffed ones with mismatched patch paint and a full rack of supplies.
I practiced saying welcome in seven accents this morning and panicked right back into my normal voice.
Note to self: never shake a pressurized coolant flask just because it makes a funny sloshing sound.
The quartermaster tracks every bolt on a green phosphor screen older than half the pilots in the bar.
Even a tiny courier feels like a palace when the galley is warm and the filter bank is humming.
A tug pilot gifted me a jar of pickled peppers from three sectors over and my eyebrows still have not forgiven him.
Check your hold capacity before signing a bulky delivery, or you will be playing crate tetris on the apron.
Training your crew costs a few shiplets up front, yet it saves headaches when things get busy mid-flight.
Survey records earn more once packaged in Science, so let the lab wrap them up on the ride into port.
Thermal Control helps steady the drive when long hauls start wearing the machinery down.
Damage Control can patch hull scrapes out of salvage and power if the next drydock is far away.
I waved both arms to guide a heavy hauler in yesterday before remembering we use automated laser rails.
Somewhere in the station vents lives a lost wrench from the last charter, rattling purely for dramatic effect.
Take a breath while you are tied up at the pier; space will still be right where you left it when you undock.
Safe skies whenever you cast off, captain, and try to bring back at least as many hull plates as you left with.
